topic.title: Communication: Measurement and evidence in Multilingual Public Information
topic.focus: how success is evaluated and why evidence can be disputed

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: In the spring of 2015, Malmö city council in southern Sweden ran a campaign urging parents to book free measles vaccinations for their children. Letters were posted to around 40,000 households, yet in several neighbourhoods fewer than one family in ten responded. When health visitors knocked on doors, they found that many parents had simply not understood the letters, which were written only in Swedish. Within six weeks, the council's communications office began translating health and emergency notices into Arabic, Somali, Persian and Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian, the four most widely spoken languages in the city after Swedish. The change was a response to a crisis rather than a planned experiment, and nobody thought to record how many residents were being reached. Systematic data collection only began in 2018. As a result, the first three years are documented mainly through the memories of translators, community liaison workers and residents – accounts that are valuable but cannot be checked against any formal record.

sections.heading: How it operates
sections.text: Today the service has grown from four languages to eight. A team of nine staff translators and fourteen part-time liaison workers converts around 1,200 official notices a year before publication. The council's evaluation relies on three sources: the number of people using council services, broken down by the language they choose on the booking system; the volume of requests for translations that do not yet exist; and complaints about missing or confusing material. None of these was designed as a measure of success. They are produced automatically as a by-product of daily work, which means they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody. The drawback is that they record what people do, not why they do it. Between 2017 and 2021, the council also funded a separate door-to-door outreach programme in some of the same neighbourhoods, and any rise in service use during those years could reflect the visits as easily as the translations.

sections.heading: Evidence and experience
sections.text: On the initiative's central claim, the evidence is reasonably strong. Bookings made by residents who select a language other than Swedish rose by 26% between 2018 and 2023, and the rise continued after the outreach programme ended, which suggests that translation was doing at least some of the work. Interviews carried out in 2022 by researchers at Malmö University point in the same direction: of 310 residents questioned, 71% said they had used a council service for the first time after reading information in their own language. Farida Osman, a liaison worker since 2016, remembers a mother who arrived at a clinic holding a translated leaflet "as if it were a ticket". The evidence on costs is far weaker. Concentrating resources on eight languages leaves speakers of less common languages – Tigrinya, Dari or Romani, for example – still largely excluded, but because these residents rarely appear in booking records or complaint logs, their exclusion is almost invisible in official reports. The imbalance, in other words, lies in how well each side is measured, not necessarily in how much each side matters.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: This creates a genuine dilemma for the five-member oversight panel that decides each year which languages receive priority. According to a 2023 survey of home languages, speakers of the next twenty most common languages make up about 6% of Malmö's residents, yet they receive almost nothing in translation. Some panel members argue that this figure proves the current eight languages are the right choice, since they cover the vast majority of residents who do not speak Swedish at home. Others point out that the smallest communities are often the most recently arrived and the least able to find help informally, so a low share of the population may conceal a high level of need. Mistakes are easy to make in both directions. In 2019 the panel dropped Turkish from the priority list because request numbers were falling, only to reinstate it eighteen months later when liaison workers reported that older Turkish speakers had stopped asking for translations because they assumed none would be provided. Yet ignoring the figures altogether is no better, because the argument is then won by whoever speaks most persuasively at the meeting.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Improving the evidence would mean paying for measurement that the service has so far managed without. A full evaluation, with surveys in every priority language and a comparison group, has been costed at roughly 2.4 million kronor – almost a fifth of the service's annual budget. Some councillors propose a cheaper route: using machine translation to cover thirty or more languages at a fraction of the cost and then measuring which ones are actually used. Professional translators object that automated tools still mishandle medical and legal terms, and that a single dangerous error could undo years of trust. A more modest step has broader support. By comparing booking figures from neighbourhoods that received outreach visits with those that did not, analysts could estimate how much of the 26% rise is due to translation alone. Such a review could be completed within one funding year, and while it would not settle every question, it would at least show how far the existing numbers can be trusted.

Paragraph 1 — Background
In the spring of 2015, Malmö city council in southern Sweden ran a campaign urging parents to book free measles vaccinations for their children. Letters were posted to around 40,000 households, yet in several neighbourhoods fewer than one family in ten responded. When health visitors knocked on doors, they found that many parents had simply not understood the letters, which were written only in Swedish. Within six weeks, the council's communications office began translating health and emergency notices into Arabic, Somali, Persian and Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian, the four most widely spoken languages in the city after Swedish. The change was a response to a crisis rather than a planned experiment, and nobody thought to record how many residents were being reached. Systematic data collection only began in 2018. As a result, the first three years are documented mainly through the memories of translators, community liaison workers and residents – accounts that are valuable but cannot be checked against any formal record.

Paragraph 2 — How it operates
Today the service has grown from four languages to eight. A team of nine staff translators and fourteen part-time liaison workers converts around 1,200 official notices a year before publication. The council's evaluation relies on three sources: the number of people using council services, broken down by the language they choose on the booking system; the volume of requests for translations that do not yet exist; and complaints about missing or confusing material. None of these was designed as a measure of success. They are produced automatically as a by-product of daily work, which means they cost almost nothing to collect and interrupt nobody. The drawback is that they record what people do, not why they do it. Between 2017 and 2021, the council also funded a separate door-to-door outreach programme in some of the same neighbourhoods, and any rise in service use during those years could reflect the visits as easily as the translations.

Paragraph 3 — Evidence and experience
On the initiative's central claim, the evidence is reasonably strong. Bookings made by residents who select a language other than Swedish rose by 26% between 2018 and 2023, and the rise continued after the outreach programme ended, which suggests that translation was doing at least some of the work. Interviews carried out in 2022 by researchers at Malmö University point in the same direction: of 310 residents questioned, 71% said they had used a council service for the first time after reading information in their own language. Farida Osman, a liaison worker since 2016, remembers a mother who arrived at a clinic holding a translated leaflet "as if it were a ticket". The evidence on costs is far weaker. Concentrating resources on eight languages leaves speakers of less common languages – Tigrinya, Dari or Romani, for example – still largely excluded, but because these residents rarely appear in booking records or complaint logs, their exclusion is almost invisible in official reports. The imbalance, in other words, lies in how well each side is measured, not necessarily in how much each side matters.

Paragraph 4 — Challenges
This creates a genuine dilemma for the five-member oversight panel that decides each year which languages receive priority. According to a 2023 survey of home languages, speakers of the next twenty most common languages make up about 6% of Malmö's residents, yet they receive almost nothing in translation. Some panel members argue that this figure proves the current eight languages are the right choice, since they cover the vast majority of residents who do not speak Swedish at home. Others point out that the smallest communities are often the most recently arrived and the least able to find help informally, so a low share of the population may conceal a high level of need. Mistakes are easy to make in both directions. In 2019 the panel dropped Turkish from the priority list because request numbers were falling, only to reinstate it eighteen months later when liaison workers reported that older Turkish speakers had stopped asking for translations because they assumed none would be provided. Yet ignoring the figures altogether is no better, because the argument is then won by whoever speaks most persuasively at the meeting.

Paragraph 5 — Next steps
Improving the evidence would mean paying for measurement that the service has so far managed without. A full evaluation, with surveys in every priority language and a comparison group, has been costed at roughly 2.4 million kronor – almost a fifth of the service's annual budget. Some councillors propose a cheaper route: using machine translation to cover thirty or more languages at a fraction of the cost and then measuring which ones are actually used. By comparing booking figures from neighbourhoods that received outreach visits with those that did not, analysts could estimate how much of the 26% rise is due to translation alone. Such a review could be completed within one funding year, and while it would not settle every question, it would at least show how far the existing numbers can be trusted.
